issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Martin Weber is a 76-year-old divorced hotel manager who came to treatment after months of feeling that his world had narrowed to a few places he could still tolerate. The event he returns to happened at the hotel where he has worked for years. During a maintenance problem in a lower service area, a toxic chemical was released. Martin remembers being in a back corridor near the service rooms when he became aware of a harsh smell and confusion around him, but his recollection does not unfold like a complete story. What he carries are broken sections: the sting of the air, the sudden sense that something was wrong, scattered movement, the sound of people shouting, and then gaps. When he tries to describe it, the sequence will not hold together for him. He says the memory comes in pieces that do not fit, and at times what returns first is not an image at all but the same surge of fear and bodily alarm he felt that day, arriving all at once, as if the event were happening in his chest before it appears in his mind.

That smell has stayed with him most vividly. Even now, when he thinks about the exposure, he can suddenly detect the scent he associates with that corridor, sharp and chemical, even when there is nothing around him that should smell that way. Those moments unsettle him deeply because they seem to prove to him that his body is not under his control. He has come to believe he can no longer trust his own body. If his breathing changes, if his stomach drops, if his skin prickles, he does not take these sensations lightly; he reads them as signs that his body is reacting as though danger is still present. He often says that his body has become an enemy to him, setting off alarms when he is supposedly safe. Alongside this is a bleak conviction that he cannot stop bad things from happening to him. At his age, he had imagined himself as seasoned and capable, someone who knew how to handle emergencies in a hotel. What frightened him most was not only the exposure itself, but the realization that something invisible in the air could overwhelm him before he had any chance to protect himself.

In the weeks after the incident, Martin returned to work, but the hotel no longer felt like familiar ground. The service corridors and the area near the event site became impossible for him to enter unless absolutely necessary, and usually he arranged matters so someone else would go. As manager, he could still direct staff from the front office or remain in more public areas, but this changed how he worked. Maintenance issues that once would have drawn him downstairs were now delegated or postponed. He told himself this was simple caution, but over time it reduced his sense of competence and increased his dependence on others for parts of the building he used to oversee himself.

Unexpected sounds now catch him immediately. A loud bang in the kitchen, the crash of dropped glassware in the bar, an alarm test, even a cart slamming into a service door can make him go rigid and scan the environment. He is particularly unsettled by abrupt noises because the event began with sudden confusion and commotion before he understood what was happening. He stays on edge even at home, where he once expected relief. If a television program changes volume suddenly, if a neighbor drops something in the hallway, if there is any sharp sound at night, he feels instantly on guard. His apartment has become one of the very few places he can tolerate, yet even there he does not feel fully at ease.

To cope, Martin keeps noise around him almost constantly. He turns on the television loudly or plays music so there is no silence in which sensations or thoughts might intrude. He also monitors his own mind closely, watching for any sign that he is “going crazy,” as he puts it. If he notices the chemical smell in his mind again, or a rush of fear without a clear picture, he begins checking himself: whether he is thinking clearly, whether he is losing his grip, whether this is what happens before someone breaks down. These private checks occupy him for long stretches of the day.

By the time he sought help, Martin’s life had contracted around work areas he considered manageable and a very small number of places he regarded as safe. What finally brought him in was the accumulating sense that he was no longer living as himself. He could still perform many duties, but only by arranging his days to avoid certain parts of the hotel and by bracing himself against sounds and bodily reactions that felt treacherous. He said he was afraid that if this continued, he would lose the last of his confidence and become trapped entirely in a shrinking safe zone. What he hopes for now is not to erase what happened, but to be able to stand in his own hotel, and in his own home, without feeling that danger is already inside him.
